GeoVax Highlights Likely Sustained Clade Ib Mpox Transmission in the United States NewMediaWire · GeoVax, Inc. NewMediaWire Tue, September 29, 2026 at 8:37 AM EDT 5 min read GOVX -0.65% CDC Reports Changing U.S. Transmission Dynamics Underscore Importance of Continued Surveillance, Vaccine Preparedness and Resilient MVA Vaccine Supply ATLANTA, GA - September 29, 2026 (NEWMEDIAWIRE) - GeoVax Labs, Inc. (Nasdaq: GOVX), a clinical-stage biotechnology company developing vaccines against infectious diseases and therapies for solid tumor cancers, today highlighted an important change in the U.S. epidemiology of Clade I mpox reported by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). In its September 25 update, CDC reported more than 60 laboratory-confirmed Clade I mpox cases across at least 20 U.S. states. Since August, an increasing proportion of U.S. Clade I cases have occurred among individuals with no recent international travel or known links to recent travelers. Cases with presumed domestic transmission have now been reported in more than 10 jurisdictions, which CDC said indicates a "likely transition to sustained Clade Ib transmission in the United States." CDC continues to assess the risk from the Clade I outbreak as low for most people in the United States, while noting that additional travel-related and domestically acquired Clade Ib cases are expected. David Dodd, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of GeoVax, commented: "CDC's latest assessment represents an important change in the epidemiology of Clade Ib mpox in the United States. While the risk to the general population remains low, presumed domestic transmission across multiple jurisdictions reinforces the importance of continued surveillance, vaccination of appropriate at-risk populations and sustained preparedness." Dodd continued: "Preparedness should not begin when an infectious-disease threat becomes a crisis. The appropriate time to strengthen vaccine capacity, diversify sources of supply and establish scalable manufacturing infrastructure is before those capabilities are urgently needed. The changing geographic footprint and public health threat of mpox is another reminder that infectious diseases do not respect national borders." Advancing GEO-MVA as a Potential Additional MVA Vaccine Option GEO-MVA is GeoVax's Modified Vaccinia Ankara (MVA)-based vaccine being developed for protection against mpox and smallpox. Following formal guidance from the European Medicines Agency (EMA), GeoVax is advancing GEO-MVA through an expedited clinical development pathway, with traditional Phase 1 and Phase 2 clinical trials not required, allowing the program to proceed directly to a pivotal Phase 3 immunobridging study comparing immune responses generated by GEO-MVA with those generated by the licensed MVA-BN comparator. GeoVax expects to initiate the 500-participant pivotal Phase 3 immunobridging study in the fourth quarter of 2026, with results expected in mid-2027, having completed the manufacturing/fill-finish and clinical operations aspects in support of initiating and completing the pivotal study. Story Continues GeoVax is developing GEO-MVA to expand global access to MVA vaccines and scalable production capabilities, with the potential to provide governments and international public health organizations with an additional source of MVA vaccine. The Company believes GEO-MVA can become an important strategic preparedness asset by supporting diversified vaccine supply, scalable manufacturing capacity and greater supply resilience, while strengthening biosecurity, orthopoxvirus preparedness and the ability to respond to evolving global health threats. Dodd concluded: "Low risk to the general population today and the need for long-term preparedness are not contradictory. CDC's latest assessment illustrates why preparedness must anticipate changes in infectious-disease transmission rather than react to them after they occur. We believe diversified vaccine supply and scalable MVA manufacturing capacity can become increasingly important as the epidemiology of mpox continues to evolve." A Changing Mpox Landscape The development is particularly noteworthy because the 2022 global mpox outbreak, including the large U.S. outbreak, was caused by Clade IIb. Clade I mpox has historically been associated with more severe disease and higher mortality than Clade II. However, disease severity varies by viral subclade, population and access to medical care. Recent Clade Ib cases identified in high-income countries have generally involved relatively mild illness, underscoring the importance of distinguishing the changing epidemiology of the virus from the immediate risk it poses to the general population. The significance of CDC's latest assessment therefore extends beyond disease severity alone. The emergence of likely sustained Clade Ib transmission represents an important change in the geographic footprint and transmission dynamics of mpox in the United States. The new CDC assessment also represents an evolution from earlier U.S. surveillance. As recently as August, CDC reported that sustained Clade Ib transmission had not been detected in the United States during 2024–2025. The September 25 assessment now indicates a likely transition toward sustained domestic transmission. Globally, Clade I outbreaks have continued in Central and Eastern Africa since late 2023, with subsequent geographic expansion beyond the region, including transmission in parts of Europe and introductions into the United States. The evolving epidemiology follows other recent public-health preparedness actions, including updated CDC vaccination recommendations for certain U.S. travelers at increased risk and international initiatives to strengthen access to mpox vaccines and outbreak-response capabilities. About GeoVax GeoVax Labs, Inc. is a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on the development of vaccines and immunotherapies addressing high-consequence infectious diseases and solid tumor cancers. GeoVax's priority program is GEO-MVA, a Modified Vaccinia Ankara (MVA)–based vaccine targeting mpox and smallpox. The program is advancing under an expedited regulatory pathway, with plans to initiate a pivotal Phase 3 clinical trial in the second half of 2026, to address critical global needs for expanded orthopoxvirus vaccine supply and biodefense preparedness. In oncology, GeoVax is developing Gedeptin(R), a gene-directed enzyme prodrug therapy (GDEPT) designed to enhance immune checkpoint inhibitor activity. Gedeptin has completed a multicenter Phase 1/2 clinical trial in advanced head and neck cancer and is being advanced into combination strategies, including planned neoadjuvant and first-line settings. GeoVax maintains a global intellectual property portfolio supporting its infectious disease and oncology programs and continues to evaluate strategic partnerships and funding opportunities aligned with its development priorities. Health EAC Partner States urged to educate citizens on monkeypox EAC • June 17, 2022 • 4 min read Mpox patient presenting rash symptoms - Courtesy East African Community Partner States have been urged to provide necessary information for their citizens to protect themselves against monkeypox and prevent the virus from spreading. This follows reports by the World Health Organization of 780 laboratory-confirmed cases of monkeypox as of 2nd June 2022. The cases have been reported to or identified by the WHO from 27 Member States across four WHO regions that are not endemic to monkeypox virus, while Monkeypox is endemic in some African countries. According to the WHO, 1,392 suspected cases of monkeypox have been reported this year until mid of May in seven African countries. Out of these, 44 cases are confirmed. This is in the 4.5 months slightly less than half the number of cases reported for the whole of last year. WHO says the sudden appearance of monkeypox in multiple countries across the world indicates the virus has been spreading undetected for some time outside the West and Central African nations where it is usually found. Christophe Bazivamo, the EAC Deputy Secretary General in charge of the Productive and Social Sectors called on the EAC to education their citizens on monkeypox to limit spread. “Because of the proximity of the EAC Partner States to some of the affected countries, it is important that we take precautionary measures to minimize its spread,” said Bazivamo. “It is important that people are given necessary information on the nature of the disease and how they can protect themselves and prevent the disease from spreading, “This will also help in avoiding unnecessary panic and stigmatization particularly now that people easily associate any disease outbreak to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic,” added Hon. Bazivamo. The DSG further emphasized on the importance of factual risk communication to communities, that provides necessary information without causing unnecessary concern, and need for stepping up surveillance. Monkeypox outbreaks are not new. The virus was first discovered in monkeys in 1958, with the first human case in the African region detected in 1970. Since then, there have been multiple outbreaks of the viral disease that can spread from animals to humans but can also spread between people. Transmission is possible through close contact with an infected person, or objects including clothes and bedsheets as well as droplets. Symptoms typically include skin rash or lesions, fever, intense headache, muscle aches, back pain, general body weakness and swollen lymph nodes and last from two to four weeks. In many patients, the symptoms are moderate and clear up on their own but severe cases and even death can occur. WHO states the case fatality ratio, or the percent of people dying compared to those diagnosed, to be around 3-6 percent. In comparison to COVID-19, which is a highly contagious disease, transmission of monkeypox is more difficult. WHO assesses the current risk posed by monkeypox to human health and for the general public as low. To reduce the risk of contracting the virus, According to WHO, people should: Avoid coming into contact with people recently diagnosed with the virus or those who may have been infected. Wear a face mask when in close contact with someone who has symptoms. Use personal protective equipment when caring for patients with confirmed or suspected monkeypox infection. Wash hands with soap and water or use alcohol-based sanitizers, especially after coming into contact with infected or infection-suspected animals or humans. Regularly wash clothing and bedsheets at high temperature Only eat meat that has been cooked thoroughly. Avoid coming into contact with sick animals that could be carrying the virus, such as rodents or non-human primates and refrain from eating or handling so-called bush meat. A person who is suspected to have contracted monkeypox should self-isolate him or herself from physical contact with others and seek medical advice immediately. The virus causing monkeypox belongs to the same group as the smallpox virus, however, it is a much milder and less deadly form of it. Vaccination against smallpox has been shown to be protective against monkeypox and a new vaccine against smallpox and monkeypox has been approved but is not yet widely available. An antiviral to treat the monkeypox virus has been recently approved in the United States of America and in the European Union. Otherwise, treatment aims to ease the symptoms and includes, for example, painkillers. analysis.brief_en: The news report highlights the World Health Organization's (WHO) call for EAC Partner States to educate citizens on monkeypox to prevent its spread. As of June 2nd, 2022, WHO reported 780 laboratory-confirmed cases across 27 Member States in four WHO regions, with 44 confirmed cases in seven African countries by mid-May 2022. The case fatality ratio is estimated at 3-6 percent, but WHO assesses the current risk to human health and the general public as low. news.content: Menu Menu Home Business Politics Nigeria International 2Open submenu Health & Wellbeing Education Life & Style Sport Editorial Backpage Close submenuInternational Africa Rest of the World Sunday, 4th October, 2026 Home Business Politics Nigeria International Africa Rest of the World Health & Wellbeing Education Life & Style Sport Editorial Backpage Search for: Breaking News Nail-biting Finale to BBNaija S11 as Temi Nkem Is Crowned Winner 3 hours ago NOSC Selects Dear Ajayi as Nigeria’s Official Submission for 99th Oscars 5 hours ago CJN: Judiciary Committed to Impartial, Fair and Timely Administration of Justice 3 days ago 186,000bpd Committed to Debt Repayment as UAE Seeks to Spread Risk on $5bn Loan 3 days ago Latest Headlines INEC to Hold World Press Conference as 2027 Elections Hit 100-Day Countdown Nail-biting Finale to BBNaija S11 as Temi Nkem Is Crowned Winner Heirs Insurance Boss Challenges Operators on Rebuilding Confidence ADC Campaign Condemns APC’s ‘Cruel Mockery’ of Amaechi, Says Tinubu’s Govt Has Failed Nigerians Global Initiative Targets Wider Access to Mpox Vaccines in Outbreak Response Nigeria | 1 month ago Shares Share Post Email Share Share Ayodeji Ake A new global initiative has been launched to improve access to mpox vaccines and ensure that countries affected by outbreaks can receive vaccines more quickly and equitably when they are needed. ReadMed Journals The initiative builds on the work of the World Health Organisation (WHO) and its partners to strengthen international coordination of vaccine supplies and improve preparedness for mpox outbreaks, particularly in countries with limited access to vaccines. At the centre of the initiative is the International Coordinating Group on Vaccine Provision (ICG), a mechanism established in 1997 following major meningitis outbreaks in Africa. ICG was created to coordinate emergency supplies of vaccines and antibiotics for countries facing major disease outbreaks. Its role is based on the recognition that although outbreaks are difficult to predict, timely vaccination can help prevent further transmission and reduce the impact of infectious diseases. Traditionally, ICG has been responsible for ensuring equitable access to licensed vaccines against cholera, meningitis, yellow fever, and Ebola virus disease during emergencies. Its responsibilities include managing global emergency vaccine stockpiles and working with partners, donors, and vaccine manufacturers to determine the size and composition of the stocks required for effective outbreak response. The expansion of the mechanism to include mpox is expected to provide a more structured approach to the distribution of mpox vaccines, particularly during emergencies when demand can rise rapidly. The move builds on measures introduced during the global mpox response. In 2024, WHO and its partners established an Access and Allocation Mechanism (AAM) specifically for mpox vaccines, treatments and diagnostic tests. AAM was designed to support the allocation of limited medical countermeasures to countries and communities where they were most urgently required. Under the new, longer-term arrangement, ICG will continue and strengthen the work initiated through the temporary mechanism. The development also follows a decision by the Gavi Board in 2025 to formally approve the establishment and financing of a global mpox vaccine stockpile under the long-standing ICG framework. ReadMed Journals The stockpile is intended to ensure that vaccine supplies can be mobilised rapidly during outbreaks instead of relying solely on vaccine procurement after an emergency has already escalated. The initiative comes amid continued concern over mpox, a viral disease that can cause fever, rash, swollen lymph nodes and painful lesions. While many people recover, severe disease and death can occur, particularly among vulnerable populations. WHO has stressed the importance of vaccination as part of a broader outbreak response that also includes surveillance, testing, case management, contact tracing, infection prevention and community engagement. The global vaccine initiative is expected to complement, rather than replace, national public health measures. Health authorities and international partners will also need to address challenges around vaccine supply, financing, delivery and equitable access to ensure that the availability of a global stockpile translates into timely vaccination on the ground. The expansion of the ICG mechanism to include mpox represents a shift from short-term emergency arrangements towards a more sustainable system for vaccine preparedness. By maintaining emergency stocks and establishing clearer mechanisms for allocation, global health agencies aim to reduce delays in responding to future mpox outbreaks and ensure that countries most affected are not left behind in accessing lifesaving vaccines. The Clement Manyathela Show Clement Manyathela 702 Mpox Department of Health The backs of the hands of a patient with mpox showing a characteristic rash during his recovery phase. Picture: BSIP via AFP A rise in confirmed Mpox cases has prompted the Department of Health to urge people to be on the lookout for symptoms. The latest update shows 22 cases have been recorded: Western Cape (18), Gauteng ( 3) and KwaZulu-Natal (1). Except for one, all patients are male. 702’s Clement Manyathela asked Dr Helen Rees, Co-chair of South Africa’s Mpox Incident Management Team to go into detail about the disease. Health and Wellness: Understanding MPOX 00:00/20:03 Health and Wellness: Understanding MPOX Clement Manyathela speaks to Prof Helen Rees, Executive Director of Wits RHI and co-chair of South Africa’s Mpox NDOH Incident Management who shares on what MPOX is, its symptoms and how to treat it. Close Modal Dialog This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button. She explained that Mpox is a virus. Following a huge outbreak in 2022 that affected over 100 countries, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern. “People might have heard it used to be called monkeypox, but monkeys don't have a lot to do with this. So, we now call it the disease Mpox.” Rees said it’s part of a family of viruses that relate to the far more severe smallpox. When Mpox affects people, it causes a range of symptoms, but commonly fever, headaches, muscle aches and feeling lousy. “But the really characteristic thing that we look for are the lesions that develop. And these lesions can be just a few and they can, in more severe cases, be quite a lot. And they start like a sort of red spot and then they grow into a pustule and then they scab over.” If you have the symptoms and the lesions, see a healthcare professional, and once diagnosed, isolate advised Rees. How do people become infected? “It's not like COVID-19, which was spread as a respiratory disease, and it spread through the air and through droplets. And it spread from person to person very easily. Mpox is much more difficult to contract because it's spread through contact, either with somebody who's got lesions.” It can also spread, although much less frequently through little particles that have come from somebody who has got Mpox. So, for example healthcare workers who are changing sheets or towels could get it, Rees said. She went into detail about how the disease is spread. “In the African region in particular, Mpox often occurs in households and is often brought in through children and then it spreads just within the household. “What we're seeing in the outbreaks that have occurred, the large outbreaks that we've seen now globally, is that we're seeing sexual transmission of Mpox. In this case, where we've got a lot of cases in the Western Cape, we're aware of the fact that this is probably within the men who have sex with men community and pretty certainly sexually transmitted through contact.” Can someone recover completely from Mpox or can the infection cause longer term health problems or complications? Rees said if you're a healthy person, you will 99.9% recover completely. “A group that we're very worried about... are people who are what we call immunocompromised. In the South African setting the commonest reason for immunocompromised when your immune system isn't robust and isn't working as well is HIV when you're not on treatment.” She added that in some cases, particularly if there are children, there can be some sequelae. “And in some cases you might see things like lesions occurring in eyes, in which case you can have sort of after effects there. But nearly everyone else will recover completely.” There are 10,000 vaccines which the Department of Health has access to. “And we're encouraging people who are either contacts, in which case go as soon as you can, and you'll get this vaccine called MVA-BN. But the other group we would encourage is people who think they're at high risk.” Are there any medicines that actually treat the virus itself or is treatment mainly about managing the symptoms while the body clears the infection? Rees said treat it just as you do if you have influenza. “Things that will bring down a fever or address muscle aches, etc. So, it really is about managing the symptoms. And obviously, if you've got a lot of lesions on your body, you need to be careful how you manage those. We don't want you to scratch them. Scratching obviously will delay healing.” She said there is one drug called Tecovirimat being used for severe cases in South Africa and globally. It's what we call an antiviral drug... but the evidence of how effective that is is slim. So at the moment, there are clinical trials going on worldwide looking for better antivirals to treat Mpox because it's becoming so common.” Never miss a major story. The Clement Manyathela Show Clement Manyathela 702 Mpox Department of Health The backs of the hands of a patient with mpox showing a characteristic rash during his recovery phase. Picture: BSIP via AFP A rise in confirmed Mpox cases has prompted the Department of Health to urge people to be on the lookout for symptoms. The latest update shows 22 cases have been recorded: Western Cape (18), Gauteng ( 3) and KwaZulu-Natal (1). Except for one, all patients are male. 702’s Clement Manyathela asked Dr Helen Rees, Co-chair of South Africa’s Mpox Incident Management Team to go into detail about the disease. Health and Wellness: Understanding MPOX 00:00/20:03 Health and Wellness: Understanding MPOX Clement Manyathela speaks to Prof Helen Rees, Executive Director of Wits RHI and co-chair of South Africa’s Mpox NDOH Incident Management who shares on what MPOX is, its symptoms and how to treat it. Following a huge outbreak in 2022 that affected over 100 countries, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern. “People might have heard it used to be called monkeypox, but monkeys don't have a lot to do with this. So, we now call it the disease Mpox.” Rees said it’s part of a family of viruses that relate to the far more severe smallpox. When Mpox affects people, it causes a range of symptoms, but commonly fever, headaches, muscle aches and feeling lousy. “But the really characteristic thing that we look for are the lesions that develop. And these lesions can be just a few and they can, in more severe cases, be quite a lot. And they start like a sort of red spot and then they grow into a pustule and then they scab over.” If you have the symptoms and the lesions, see a healthcare professional, and once diagnosed, isolate advised Rees. How do people become infected? “It's not like COVID-19, which was spread as a respiratory disease, and it spread through the air and through droplets. And it spread from person to person very easily. Mpox is much more difficult to contract because it's spread through contact, either with somebody who's got lesions.” It can also spread, although much less frequently through little particles that have come from somebody who has got Mpox. So, for example healthcare workers who are changing sheets or towels could get it, Rees said. She went into detail about how the disease is spread. “In the African region in particular, Mpox often occurs in households and is often brought in through children and then it spreads just within the household. “What we're seeing in the outbreaks that have occurred, the large outbreaks that we've seen now globally, is that we're seeing sexual transmission of Mpox. In this case, where we've got a lot of cases in the Western Cape, we're aware of the fact that this is probably within the men who have sex with men community and pretty certainly sexually transmitted through contact.” Can someone recover completely from Mpox or can the infection cause longer term health problems or complications? Rees said if you're a healthy person, you will 99.9% recover completely. “A group that we're very worried about... are people who are what we call immunocompromised. In the South African setting the commonest reason for immunocompromised when your immune system isn't robust and isn't working as well is HIV when you're not on treatment.” She added that in some cases, particularly if there are children, there can be some sequelae. “And in some cases you might see things like lesions occurring in eyes, in which case you can have sort of after effects there. But nearly everyone else will recover completely.” There are 10,000 vaccines which the Department of Health has access to. “And we're encouraging people who are either contacts, in which case go as soon as you can, and you'll get this vaccine called MVA-BN. But the other group we would encourage is people who think they're at high risk.” Are there any medicines that actually treat the virus itself or is treatment mainly about managing the symptoms while the body clears the infection? Rees said treat it just as you do if you have influenza. “Things that will bring down a fever or address muscle aches, etc. So, it really is about managing the symptoms. And obviously, if you've got a lot of lesions on your body, you need to be careful how you manage those. We don't want you to scratch them. Scratching obviously will delay healing.” She said there is one drug called Tecovirimat being used for severe cases in South Africa and globally. It's what we call an antiviral drug... but the evidence of how effective that is is slim. So at the moment, there are clinical trials going on worldwide looking for better antivirals to treat Mpox because it's becoming so common.” Never miss a major story. news.content: Home » News » Measles, not mpox, reported at Bayview store, owner says Measles, not mpox, reported at Bayview store, owner says Lauren O’Connor May | 29 Sep 2026 Share this article: Measles, not mpox, reported at Bayview store, owner says Lauren O’Connor May | 29 Sep 2026 Share this article: A Bayview store has confirmed that the monkeypox rumour circulating on social media is false. This comes after a voicenote shared on community WhatsApp groups over the weekend claimed that staff at the OK store in Spine Road had contacted the infectious disease but the store was not closed. The note alleged that “all the cashiers were sent home” with confirmed cases of “monkeypox”, a term which the World Health Organisation phased out in favour of mpox, due to stigma. National outbreak Panic quickly spread after dozens of cases of the disease were confirmed in the province in recent weeks. The national Department of Health has issued an alert to citizens to be vigilant after a sharp increase in laboratory-confirmed mpox cases over the past few weeks, with the Western Cape recording the highest number of cases. Measles mistaken The panic was unwarranted, though, as OK Bayview store owner Ettiene Nel confirmed that while several staff members had been booked off sick, doctors’ notes confirmed that they had measles and not mpox. He said that the store immediately sends all ill employees to the doctor to confirm whether they are fit to work and that no mpox cases had been reported at the store. “There is no one at work that is contagious,” he said. Health department confirms Western Cape Department of Health and Wellness (WCDHW) spokesperson Dwayne Evans said there have been no confirmed cases of mpox in Strandfontein. “We appeal to the public to not spread unverified information and encourage them to follow our official social media channels and reputable media sources,” he said. What is mpox? According to the national alert, mpox is a viral disease. Symptoms include fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, fatigue and rash or skin lesions. “Typically, the skin lesions start as flat red spots before progressing to bumps, followed by fluid-filled blisters, then pus filled bumps and eruptions into crusted scabs. The symptoms usually appear within 6 to 13 days after exposure but can range from 5 to 21 days. Therefore, anyone experiencing these symptoms, particularly if they have had close contact with a confirmed case or a suspected case, should seek medical attention immediately and avoid close contact with others,” the health department said in the alert. “Mpox is transmitted mainly through close physical contact with an infected person, including skin-to-skin contact with the rash or lesions, and contact with contaminated materials such as bedding, clothing, or towels used by an infected person. “Mpox-positive persons can also transmit the virus through respiratory droplets during prolonged face-to-face contact, uncovered coughing or sneezing,” it said. The alert urged vigilance and advised frequent hand washing as a preventative measure. “The government, through the support of the World Health Organization, has secured limited doses of mpox vaccines (MVA-BN) and treatment (Tecovirimat) as part of its outbreak response strategy to disrupt local transmission,” the alert said. news.content_original: Home » News » Measles, not mpox, reported at Bayview store, owner says Measles, not mpox, reported at Bayview store, owner says Lauren O’Connor May | 29 Sep 2026 Share this article: Measles, not mpox, reported at Bayview store, owner says Lauren O’Connor May | 29 Sep 2026 Share this article: A Bayview store has confirmed that the monkeypox rumour circulating on social media is false. This comes after a voicenote shared on community WhatsApp groups over the weekend claimed that staff at the OK store in Spine Road had contacted the infectious disease but the store was not closed. The note alleged that “all the cashiers were sent home” with confirmed cases of “monkeypox”, a term which the World Health Organisation phased out in favour of mpox, due to stigma. National outbreak Panic quickly spread after dozens of cases of the disease were confirmed in the province in recent weeks. The national Department of Health has issued an alert to citizens to be vigilant after a sharp increase in laboratory-confirmed mpox cases over the past few weeks, with the Western Cape recording the highest number of cases. Measles mistaken The panic was unwarranted, though, as OK Bayview store owner Ettiene Nel confirmed that while several staff members had been booked off sick, doctors’ notes confirmed that they had measles and not mpox. He said that the store immediately sends all ill employees to the doctor to confirm whether they are fit to work and that no mpox cases had been reported at the store. “There is no one at work that is contagious,” he said. Health department confirms Western Cape Department of Health and Wellness (WCDHW) spokesperson Dwayne Evans said there have been no confirmed cases of mpox in Strandfontein. “We appeal to the public to not spread unverified information and encourage them to follow our official social media channels and reputable media sources,” he said. What is mpox? According to the national alert, mpox is a viral disease. Symptoms include fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, fatigue and rash or skin lesions. “Typically, the skin lesions start as flat red spots before progressing to bumps, followed by fluid-filled blisters, then pus filled bumps and eruptions into crusted scabs. The symptoms usually appear within 6 to 13 days after exposure but can range from 5 to 21 days. Therefore, anyone experiencing these symptoms, particularly if they have had close contact with a confirmed case or a suspected case, should seek medical attention immediately and avoid close contact with others,” the health department said in the alert. “Mpox is transmitted mainly through close physical contact with an infected person, including skin-to-skin contact with the rash or lesions, and contact with contaminated materials such as bedding, clothing, or towels used by an infected person. “Mpox-positive persons can also transmit the virus through respiratory droplets during prolonged face-to-face contact, uncovered coughing or sneezing,” it said. The alert urged vigilance and advised frequent hand washing as a preventative measure. “The government, through the support of the World Health Organization, has secured limited doses of mpox vaccines (MVA-BN) and treatment (Tecovirimat) as part of its outbreak response strategy to disrupt local transmission,” the alert said. news.content_title: Monkeypox Confirmed in Congo’s Ebola-Hit Bunia as Health Officials Brace for More Cases
news.content: Monkeypox Confirmed in Congo’s Ebola-Hit Bunia as Health Officials Brace for More Cases Five other potential cases are being investigated as the U.S. spends another $267 million to the region for the battle against Ebola. Just in time to mark the start of the Halloween season, comes news that Monkeypox is teaming up with Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). This week, health officials are confirming a case of Monkeypox in Bunia, in the DRC’s Ituri province. This region is already responding to a major Ebola outbreak. - The epidemic caused by the Ebola outbreak was declared on May 15 in Ituri province, where Bunia is located, and has infected 7,890 people and killed 3,799, according to government data published on Thursday. - Mpox is a viral disease that causes fever and skin lesions and spreads through close physical contact. - Congo declared an end to mpox as a national public health emergency in April after a three-year outbreak that resulted in more than 34,000 confirmed cases nationwide. Authorities cautioned at the time that the virus had not been eradicated and could resurge. - The latest case involves a 21-year-old woman who was admitted to hospital on Thursday with lesions across her body consistent with mpox, hospital director Davin Ambitapio Musungufu said. She tested positive on Friday, he and two health officials told Reuters. Reports indicate that five other suspected Monkeypox cases in Bunia are currently under investigation This week, the U.S. announced it would send another $267 million to help contain the Ebola outbreak in the DRC. The money is intended for treatment units, safe-burial teams, protective and medical supplies, surveillance, and contact tracing. This brings the total amount our country has provided for this response to $886 million. Our State Department hopes that other UN members do more to address these outbreaks than redo world maps. Senior State Department officials announced the funding on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, hoping for pledges of new funds from other countries to meet a target of $2 billion to fight the disease, mainly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The outbreak was detected in May and is already the second most lethal on record, behind one in West Africa from 2014 to 2016. On Wednesday, Congolese Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka described the outbreak as a “major test” for the country. “For the DRC, fighting this epidemic is an absolute priority. After having contained 16 previous outbreaks, the DRC is mobilizing recognized scientific and operational expertise. And thanks to national mobilization and the support of our partners, the response has recently begun producing tangible results,” she told the United Nations General Assembly. The US pledge on Wednesday brings the Trump administration’s commitment to tackling the outbreak to $886 million, including $107 million from the Department of Health and Human Services in addition to State Department funding. At least the British are trying to help. A rare form of Ebola, known as the Bundibugyo species, is spreading rapidly in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where more than 7,800 people have caught the virus since May, 3,700 of whom have died. To prepare for the threat of imported cases, Britain has positioned three experts in and around the South Sudanese capital, Juba. They will assist and train local authorities on infection control, set up awareness campaigns for local communities, and test people crossing the border for the virus. ...Experts fear it is only a matter of time before the virus spreads to South Sudan, which shares a 500-mile border with the DRC. Thousands of people cross the frontier each day to work, attend school and trade goods, mostly fish, in lucrative markets between the two countries. If the virus gained a foothold in South Sudan, which became the newest country on earth after severing ties with Khartoum in 2011, experts fear the consequences would be catastrophic and worsen an already dire humanitarian situation. Halloween may be weeks away, but the public-health nightmare in the DRC needs no costumes or special effects. With Monkeypox now confirmed in Bunia amid the Ebola response, surveillance, treatment, and help from neighboring countries matter far more than another round of UN pageantry. news.content_original: Monkeypox Confirmed in Congo’s Ebola-Hit Bunia as Health Officials Brace for More Cases Five other potential cases are being investigated as the U.S. spends another $267 million to the region for the battle against Ebola. Just in time to mark the start of the Halloween season, comes news that Monkeypox is teaming up with Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). This week, health officials are confirming a case of Monkeypox in Bunia, in the DRC’s Ituri province. This region is already responding to a major Ebola outbreak. - The epidemic caused by the Ebola outbreak was declared on May 15 in Ituri province, where Bunia is located, and has infected 7,890 people and killed 3,799, according to government data published on Thursday. - Mpox is a viral disease that causes fever and skin lesions and spreads through close physical contact. - Congo declared an end to mpox as a national public health emergency in April after a three-year outbreak that resulted in more than 34,000 confirmed cases nationwide. Authorities cautioned at the time that the virus had not been eradicated and could resurge. - The latest case involves a 21-year-old woman who was admitted to hospital on Thursday with lesions across her body consistent with mpox, hospital director Davin Ambitapio Musungufu said. She tested positive on Friday, he and two health officials told Reuters. Reports indicate that five other suspected Monkeypox cases in Bunia are currently under investigation This week, the U.S. announced it would send another $267 million to help contain the Ebola outbreak in the DRC. The money is intended for treatment units, safe-burial teams, protective and medical supplies, surveillance, and contact tracing. This brings the total amount our country has provided for this response to $886 million. Our State Department hopes that other UN members do more to address these outbreaks than redo world maps. Senior State Department officials announced the funding on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, hoping for pledges of new funds from other countries to meet a target of $2 billion to fight the disease, mainly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The outbreak was detected in May and is already the second most lethal on record, behind one in West Africa from 2014 to 2016. On Wednesday, Congolese Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka described the outbreak as a “major test” for the country. “For the DRC, fighting this epidemic is an absolute priority. After having contained 16 previous outbreaks, the DRC is mobilizing recognized scientific and operational expertise. And thanks to national mobilization and the support of our partners, the response has recently begun producing tangible results,” she told the United Nations General Assembly. The US pledge on Wednesday brings the Trump administration’s commitment to tackling the outbreak to $886 million, including $107 million from the Department of Health and Human Services in addition to State Department funding. At least the British are trying to help. A rare form of Ebola, known as the Bundibugyo species, is spreading rapidly in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where more than 7,800 people have caught the virus since May, 3,700 of whom have died. To prepare for the threat of imported cases, Britain has positioned three experts in and around the South Sudanese capital, Juba. They will assist and train local authorities on infection control, set up awareness campaigns for local communities, and test people crossing the border for the virus. ...Experts fear it is only a matter of time before the virus spreads to South Sudan, which shares a 500-mile border with the DRC. Thousands of people cross the frontier each day to work, attend school and trade goods, mostly fish, in lucrative markets between the two countries. If the virus gained a foothold in South Sudan, which became the newest country on earth after severing ties with Khartoum in 2011, experts fear the consequences would be catastrophic and worsen an already dire humanitarian situation. Halloween may be weeks away, but the public-health nightmare in the DRC needs no costumes or special effects. With Monkeypox now confirmed in Bunia amid the Ebola response, surveillance, treatment, and help from neighboring countries matter far more than another round of UN pageantry. Let’s hope the promised funding and supplies reach the people fighting these outbreaks before either virus delivers a more frightening October surprise. Minister Mai said the case is of a 31-year-old Ugandan man residing at Juba’s Kopuri suburb and is being managed by a team of health experts at Gudele Hospital. “The Ministry of Health would like to notify the general public about the declaration of an outbreak of the Mpox in South Sudan. This outbreak is declared following a confirmation by the National Public Health Laboratory on Feb 6,” he announced. “Sample collected from a 31-year-old male, a Ugandan national and a resident of Kafuri camp at Luri Payam, Juba.” The acting health minister narrated that the patient presented with fever, rash and body itching with symptom onset on 22nd January 2025. Dr. Kidiende Chong, Director General of Preventive Health Services and Emergency Response, said the ministry has mobilized a team of expert who are currently investigating the incident and tracing possible contacts. “We have the first case which we investigated and confirmed and we mobilized the team of experts that are currently investigating and the report will be out,” he said. “Once the report is out, we’ll be able to let the public know if there is any possible case that will be detected. But be rest assured, all the possible contacts are going to be enlisted and they will be investigated.” World Health Organization (WHO) Representative for South Sudan Dr. Humphrey Karamagi said the patient starting becoming ill on Thursday afternoon, and commended the health ministry for its swift response. Dr. Karamagi reiterated that Mpox is a public health emergency of international concern, and promised to work with South Sudan government in combating the outbreak. Mpox is an infectious disease that can cause a painful rash, enlarged lymph nodes, fever, headache, muscle ache, back pain and low energy. It is said to spread from person to person mainly through close contact with someone who has mpox, including members of a household. South Sudan has been on high alert since August 2024 when the new strain was recorded among some of its neighbors including Kenya, Uganda, DRC, and Central Africa Republic. news.title_zh: 南苏丹宣布 猴痘 暴发 - Eye Radio
news.source_body_en: South Sudan has declared an Mpox outbreak following the confirmation of its first case in Juba on February 6, 2025. The patient, a 31-year-old Ugandan man residing in the Kopuri suburb and Kafuri camp at Luri Payam, presented with fever, rash, and body itching, with symptom onset on January 22, 2025. Acting Health Minister James Hoth Mai announced the outbreak in a press conference on February 7, 2025, emphasizing the need for public awareness. The Ministry of Health has mobilized a team of experts to investigate the incident and trace possible contacts, while the World Health Organization (WHO) Representative for South Sudan, Dr. Humphrey Karamagi, commended the swift response and reiterated that Mpox is a public health emergency of international concern. The outbreak remains under investigation, with further reports expected as the team continues its work.
news.content_zh: 南苏丹于 2025 年 2 月 6 日在朱巴确诊首例病例后,宣布为 猴痘 暴发。患者是一名 31 岁乌干达男子,居住在 Kopuri 郊区和 Luri Payam 的 Kafuri 营地,出现发烧、皮疹和身体瘙痒,症状于 2025 年 1 月 22 日发病。代理卫生部长 James Hoth Mai 宣布暴发在2025年2月7日的新闻发布会上强调了公众意识的必要性。卫生部已动员专家小组调查这一事件并追踪可能的接触者,世界卫生组织(WHO)南苏丹代表汉弗莱·卡拉马吉博士赞扬了南苏丹的迅速反应,并重申猴痘是国际关注的突发公共卫生事件。暴发 仍在调查中,随着团队继续工作,预计会有进一步的报告。

news.content: Abstract Pathogen genomics has become increasingly integrated into outbreak response, with recent virus epidemics better characterized by large numbers of viral genetic sequences. Effective international communication of viral diversity requires a scalable, adaptable nomenclature, and existing systems may not accommodate rapid sequence generation. The Pango lineage nomenclature system was designed to address these problems and has been applied to SARS-CoV-2 since early 2020. Here we generalize the underlying principles into a framework for virus surveillance. Lineages are defined as epidemiologically meaningful clusters on a phylogenetic tree, initiated from founding lineages and expanded across a phylogeny through a hierarchical system of alphanumeric sublineage names. Six years on from the inception of the Pango system, we discuss challenges and considerations for implementation. We present a Pango lineage framework for chikungunya virus, providing an alternative to the geography-based clade system and designating 21 lineages across 8 founding lineages. This generalization provides a foundation for future genomic surveillance of many viruses, including for emerging outbreaks and the surveillance of endemic pathogens. Similar content being viewed by others Main The last decade has seen an enormous increase in the generation of virus genome sequence data and characterized virus diversity, and virus genomics has become a core pillar of the surveillance of both endemic and emergent viruses. Systems of virus nomenclature and classification are required to organize and make sense of this genomic information. The International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses classifies viruses down to the species rank1. Description of viral diversity below the species rank has been historically undertaken by the scientific community, and virus variation has been subdivided using a wide variety of terms including type, subtype, genotype, group and clade (Extended Data Table 1)2,3,4. These naming systems typically categorize virus genetic diversity using a phylogenetic tree that is split into a set of clades (monophyletic or paraphyletic groups). The clades are often approximately equally divergent and well supported, thereby capturing persistent groups and enabling robust classification on a scale of months or years. However, heterogeneity among virus species in genetic diversity, in the evolutionary processes driving that diversity and in the availability of genomic data has led to a proliferation of classification systems across viral families. Many such systems were designed when far fewer viral genomes were available and may not provide sufficient granularity with the current pace and scale of virus genome generation. Genomic sequencing during the COVID-19 pandemic has yielded to date more than 17 million publicly shared virus genomes and supported global real-time tracking of the virus’ evolution and spread. Public health actions during the pandemic were directly informed by virus genomics, and a critical enabler of this was the use of shared systems for naming virus genetic diversity, which facilitated unambiguous communication about virus clusters and variants worldwide. In 2020, Rambaut et al. proposed a dynamic nomenclature for SARS-CoV-2 lineages, called Pango, which was designed as a real-time framework for categorizing virus genetic diversity at a high level of phylogenetic resolution5. Over the subsequent years, a voluntary community has curated thousands of Pango lineages from the >17 million SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences, with the aim of capturing and characterizing the leading edge of the pandemic and achieving a globally consistent horizon scanning framework6,7. The widespread adoption of the Pango lineage nomenclature for SARS-CoV-2, coupled with substantial increases in global sequencing capacity as a result of the pandemic, has led to the development of similar lineage systems for other viruses, including mpox virus (MPXV)8, rabies virus9, human respiratory syncytial virus10 and dengue virus11. As genomics becomes a fully integrated component of viral outbreak response and surveillance, many other viruses will require a fine-scale nomenclature capable of categorizing epidemiologically relevant diversity12. Here we outline the key principles of a unified dynamic virus lineage system that formalizes and generalizes the Pango lineage nomenclature. We highlight the applications that are most amenable to a Pango-style nomenclature framework and offer practical guidance for implementation. We present this framework with genomic epidemiology in mind, although Pango lineages could also be applied to well-sampled non-human outbreaks in the case of epizootics. Results Principles of a Pango lineage system nomenclature A Pango lineage nomenclature aims to capture the epidemiologically relevant diversity of a given pathogen on the phylogenetic scale that is most informative to address public health questions. Any such system should therefore be established with a clear public health or evolutionary objective in mind—such as informing control or eradication efforts, tracking outbreak transmission dynamics or monitoring viral evolution in response to new vaccines or therapeutics. By providing a common language for describing emerging viral clusters, a nomenclature system enables consistent communication across institutions, regions and national borders. It can serve as a practical approach to the phylogenetic placement of newly generated virus genomes when datasets are exceptionally large or when users lack the computational resources or time to reconstruct phylogenetic trees de novo, thus enabling rapid data interpretation and decision-making. A Pango lineage is a set of virus sequences that form an epidemiologically relevant cluster on a phylogenetic tree. The data in question can represent either complete genomes or partial genome sequences; however, greater granularity will be achieved if complete genomes are used13. A range of signals may justify the definition of a new lineage, depending on the epidemiology, evolution and socio-medical context of the virus in question. Possible signals include (1) introduction into a new region with onward transmission, (2) changes in phenotype, (3) a notable set (constellation) of mutations that may have phenotypic relevance, (4) recombination or reassortment or (5) evidence of rapid growth relative to other lineages (Fig. 1a). Depending on the virus and its context, only some of these, or distinct, signals may be relevant. For SARS-CoV-2, early lineage definitions were informed by geographical clustering, as movement of people was limited owing to travel restrictions14,15. As the pandemic progressed and global travel resumed, lineage criteria shifted to other epidemiologically relevant signals, including growth advantage, recombination and mutations associated with possible immune escape or vaccine evasion16,17,18,19. In the Pango lineage system, sets of sequences and a phylogenetic tree are used to define which sequences belong to which lineage (Fig. 1b). The system discriminates between two different modes of categorization: designation and assignment. In the designation process, a set of designated sequences are defined, which represent a curated subset of high-quality sequences that definitively and unambiguously belong to that lineage. Thus, the designated sequences form a canonical reference set for a lineage within a given Pango lineage system (although summary information, such as defining mutations, may also accompany this definition). For any given phylogenetic tree, the designated sequences define the scope of the phylogenetic clade of the given lineage. In some cases, the designated sequences will comprise all the genomes within a lineage; however, in many cases, the designated sequences will comprise only a fraction of the total lineage. This will depend on the rate of data generation. When data generation is slow, all high-quality sequences can be feasibly designated. However, for very large or rapidly changing datasets, only a small fraction of new genomes will be designated, with the remainder classified through assignment tools (as was the case for SARS-CoV-2). Sequences that are not designated to a lineage can still be classified through a different process called assignment. Assignment is performed by one or more of a range of methods, including traditional phylogenetics or time-saving approaches such as phylogenetic placement, assessment of defining mutations or machine learning-based classifiers7,20,21. The assignment process is an inferential procedure and therefore carries some uncertainty; it is possible (although unwelcome) for different assignment methods to give different classification results, and this uncertainty should be accounted for when interpreting the results. In addition, assignment may be performed on lower-quality or incomplete sequences, whereas only high-quality sequences are suitable for designation. Definition of a Pango lineage A lineage is defined formally as all viruses that subtend from the most recent common ancestor defined by the set of designated sequences (Fig. 1b). A new lineage must meet the following criteria (Fig. 1c): - 1. It is genetically distinct from the ancestral lineage by one or more mutations. - 2. It has epidemiological relevance, as assessed by a previously defined set of relevant signals. - 3. There is evidence of onward community transmission. - 4. There are a sufficient number of high-quality genomes to evaluate these criteria. The exact thresholds for these criteria will necessarily differ among viruses owing to differences in evolutionary rates, sequencing intensity, the length of time the virus has been circulating in humans and public health use cases. For example, the number of mutations that separate a new lineage from its ancestral diversity may be lower in slower-evolving viruses, or when fine-scale resolution is needed, and the number of genomes required to define a lineage may depend on the volume of data available for a given outbreak. Specific criteria and thresholds should be set for each virus or use case, but can be applied flexibly to allow for unforeseen circumstances, and may also change through time as the epidemiological context changes. A generalized framework for Pango lineages A Pango lineage system provides a hierarchical partition of a phylogenetic tree for a given virus, with the explicit goal of supporting genomic epidemiology for public health (Fig. 2). A lineage system is anchored on a set of founding lineages present at an initial time point of interest. For SARS-CoV-2, the earliest sequenced genomes were grouped into two founding lineages, A and B, distinguished by two mutations, which were later found to correspond to a scenario of at least two separate introductions of the virus into the human population22. For the sustained human outbreak of clade IIb MPXV, a single founding lineage, A, captured the initial diversity5,8. For any Pango lineage system, we recommend choosing an initial time point to divide existing viral diversity into one or more founding lineages, each labelled with an alphabetic code on a phylogeny (Fig. 3a,b). In the case of zoonotic spillover giving rise to a human outbreak, it would be intuitive to use the point of spillover as the initial time point. For endemic viruses with pre-existing genetic diversity, the starting point should capture currently circulating diversity while excluding extinct lineages in order to minimize complexity and reduce the burden of characterizing historic data (Fig. 3). Nomenclature systems that are less granular and use more persistent lineage labels may be better suited to describing longer-term endemic diversity. Genetic diversity that predates the chosen initial time point can be treated as ‘outside’ the nomenclature system (O). There is no requirement for Pango lineages to be similar in size, nor a need to designate all pre-existing diversity. Any undesignated diversity that later becomes relevant for public health can be added to the Pango lineage system as an additional founding lineage (Fig. 3c). Given the set of founding lineages, the designation of further descendant lineages is thereafter guided by the lineage designation rules and associated genotypic and epidemiological criteria (Fig. 3d). In situations where an established clade system already exists, the founding lineages for a Pango-style system may align directly with existing nomenclature labels, which may be particularly useful for re-emerging outbreaks of an endemic pathogen. Lineage names follow a dot-separated alphanumeric structure that encodes local phylogenetic (ancestor–descendant) relationships (Fig. 2). A new sublineage is defined by appending a dot and the next available number (for example, the 75th sublineage of BA.2 to be designated becomes BA.2.75). The names themselves should not attempt to encode any other features, such as phenotypic information or specific mutations; these features can be stored in associated metadata entries for each lineage. To maintain lineage name readability as the virus diversifies, an alias is introduced at a defined hierarchical level. SARS-CoV-2 lineages adopt an alias after three levels, whereas the MPXV system introduces an alias following two. The alias replaces the entire prefix using the next available alphabetic code (excluding X, I and O, which are reserved letters). Once all single letters have been applied, aliases will be formed using two letters; these aliases continue to be incremented alphabetically with the right-hand-most letter incremented first. For example, AA is the first alias following Z, while AB immediately follows AA, and BA immediately follows AZ. Should aliases of greater length than two letters be required, their alphabetic incrementation begins with the right-hand-most letter and proceeds with letters from right to left. When a circulating recombinant is identified, a new founding lineage is designated with the next alphabetic code prefixed with an X (Fig. 3d). For example, SARS-CoV-2 lineage XBB is a recombinant of BJ.1 (BA.2.10.1.1) and BA.2.75 (BA.2.75.3.1.1.1), and the next circulating recombinant identified and designated following XBB would be XBC, and so on. Knowing the number and exact location of precise recombination breakpoints is not required for designation, although they should be recorded where known in the associated lineage metadata entry. Note that designation can proceed even when there is uncertainty in the identification of the parental lineages of a recombinant lineage. For reassorting viruses, in which virus genome segments follow distinct evolutionary ancestries, a Pango lineage nomenclature can be anchored to a single representative segment. The choice of segment can be adapted for the intended application; for example, an appropriate choice for genomic epidemiology will be the one most relevant for transmission or antigenicity, which is often the fastest evolving and can provide the most resolution over short timescales. Reassortment of the other segments that are epidemiologically relevant could trigger a new lineage designation, an event that could be specifically encoded in the phylogeny of the representative segment for assignment purposes. Broader clade nomenclatures can track the diversity of the other segments and inform the identification of reassortants23,24. Because the goal of Pango is to capture the emerging edge of an outbreak, the phylogeny and lineage definitions must remain dynamic in response to the discovery of new information (Fig. 3c). Lineages can be withdrawn from use if, in the light of additional data or new epidemiological information, their designation criteria are no longer met (any such lineage names should be permanently deprecated and never reused). Lineages can also be split if a previously monophyletic group subsequently resolves into multiple epidemiologically relevant clusters or revised to include different sequences following new sampling. This flexibility allows early action, rather than waiting for stable clades to form through further ongoing transmission and evolution. For SARS-CoV-2 lineages, minor revisions were often needed to refine definitions as new data were shared; however, these definitions were available to the research community much more rapidly as a result of a willingness to act early and review them. Granularity of a Pango-style nomenclature No single nomenclature can serve all purposes, and a Pango lineage system is not intended to supersede existing taxonomy. Rather, it functions as a complementary framework alongside naming schemes with different granularities and timeliness. For endemic pathogen surveillance that largely samples deep, historic diversity, a fine-scale lineage nomenclature such as Pango may be of limited utility. Traditional phylogenetic analyses and clade-based nomenclatures, which incorporate minimum size and persistence criteria, are better suited to capturing long-term evolutionary patterns such as antigenic turnover8,23. In these contexts, a fine-scale system may introduce unnecessary complexity by overcategorizing the phylogenetic diversity without a clear benefit to public health. However, a Pango lineage system may be valuable for endemic pathogens in cases when new selective pressures are expected to shape short-term evolution, such as following the introduction of a novel vaccine or antiviral treatment (for example, dengue virus or respiratory syncytial virus), or when eradication programmes require close tracking of contemporary transmission (for example, measles virus or poliovirus). A Pango approach is especially well suited for outbreaks following a zoonotic spillover, for which emerging pathogen diversity should be tracked in real time. The choice of segment can be adapted for the intended application; for example, an appropriate choice for genomic epidemiology will be the one most relevant for transmission or antigenicity, which is often the fastest evolving and can provide the most resolution over short timescales. Reassortment of the other segments that are epidemiologically relevant could trigger a new lineage designation, an event that could be specifically encoded in the phylogeny of the representative segment for assignment purposes. Broader clade nomenclatures can track the diversity of the other segments and inform the identification of reassortants23,24. Because the goal of Pango is to capture the emerging edge of an outbreak, the phylogeny and lineage definitions must remain dynamic in response to the discovery of new information (Fig. 3c). Lineages can be withdrawn from use if, in the light of additional data or new epidemiological information, their designation criteria are no longer met (any such lineage names should be permanently deprecated and never reused). Lineages can also be split if a previously monophyletic group subsequently resolves into multiple epidemiologically relevant clusters or revised to include different sequences following new sampling. This flexibility allows early action, rather than waiting for stable clades to form through further ongoing transmission and evolution. For SARS-CoV-2 lineages, minor revisions were often needed to refine definitions as new data were shared; however, these definitions were available to the research community much more rapidly as a result of a willingness to act early and review them. Granularity of a Pango-style nomenclature No single nomenclature can serve all purposes, and a Pango lineage system is not intended to supersede existing taxonomy. Rather, it functions as a complementary framework alongside naming schemes with different granularities and timeliness. For endemic pathogen surveillance that largely samples deep, historic diversity, a fine-scale lineage nomenclature such as Pango may be of limited utility. Traditional phylogenetic analyses and clade-based nomenclatures, which incorporate minimum size and persistence criteria, are better suited to capturing long-term evolutionary patterns such as antigenic turnover8,23. In these contexts, a fine-scale system may introduce unnecessary complexity by overcategorizing the phylogenetic diversity without a clear benefit to public health. However, a Pango lineage system may be valuable for endemic pathogens in cases when new selective pressures are expected to shape short-term evolution, such as following the introduction of a novel vaccine or antiviral treatment (for example, dengue virus or respiratory syncytial virus), or when eradication programmes require close tracking of contemporary transmission (for example, measles virus or poliovirus). A Pango approach is especially well suited for outbreaks following a zoonotic spillover, for which emerging pathogen diversity should be tracked in real time. GeoVax Highlights Likely Sustained Clade Ib Mpox Transmission in the United States NewMediaWire · GeoVax, Inc. NewMediaWire Tue, September 29, 2026 at 8:37 AM EDT 5 min read GOVX CDC Reports Changing U.S. Transmission Dynamics Underscore Importance of Continued Surveillance, Vaccine Preparedness and Resilient MVA Vaccine Supply ATLANTA, GA - September 29, 2026 (NEWMEDIAWIRE) - GeoVax Labs, Inc. (Nasdaq: GOVX), a clinical-stage biotechnology company developing vaccines against infectious diseases and therapies for solid tumor cancers, today highlighted an important change in the U.S. epidemiology of Clade I mpox reported by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). In its September 25 update, CDC reported more than 60 laboratory-confirmed Clade I mpox cases across at least 20 U.S. states. Since August, an increasing proportion of U.S. Clade I cases have occurred among individuals with no recent international travel or known links to recent travelers. Cases with presumed domestic transmission have now been reported in more than 10 jurisdictions, which CDC said indicates a "likely transition to sustained Clade Ib transmission in the United States." CDC continues to assess the risk from the Clade I outbreak as low for most people in the United States, while noting that additional travel-related and domestically acquired Clade Ib cases are expected. David Dodd, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of GeoVax, commented: "CDC's latest assessment represents an important change in the epidemiology of Clade Ib mpox in the United States. While the risk to the general population remains low, presumed domestic transmission across multiple jurisdictions reinforces the importance of continued surveillance, vaccination of appropriate at-risk populations and sustained preparedness." Dodd continued: "Preparedness should not begin when an infectious-disease threat becomes a crisis. The appropriate time to strengthen vaccine capacity, diversify sources of supply and establish scalable manufacturing infrastructure is before those capabilities are urgently needed. The changing geographic footprint and public health threat of mpox is another reminder that infectious diseases do not respect national borders." Advancing GEO-MVA as a Potential Additional MVA Vaccine Option GEO-MVA is GeoVax's Modified Vaccinia Ankara (MVA)-based vaccine being developed for protection against mpox and smallpox. Following formal guidance from the European Medicines Agency (EMA), GeoVax is advancing GEO-MVA through an expedited clinical development pathway, with traditional Phase 1 and Phase 2 clinical trials not required, allowing the program to proceed directly to a pivotal Phase 3 immunobridging study comparing immune responses generated by GEO-MVA with those generated by the licensed MVA-BN comparator. GeoVax expects to initiate the 500-participant pivotal Phase 3 immunobridging study in the fourth quarter of 2026, with results expected in mid-2027, having completed the manufacturing/fill-finish and clinical operations aspects in support of initiating and completing the pivotal study. Story Continues GeoVax is developing GEO-MVA to expand global access to MVA vaccines and scalable production capabilities, with the potential to provide governments and international public health organizations with an additional source of MVA vaccine. The Company believes GEO-MVA can become an important strategic preparedness asset by supporting diversified vaccine supply, scalable manufacturing capacity and greater supply resilience, while strengthening biosecurity, orthopoxvirus preparedness and the ability to respond to evolving global health threats. Dodd concluded: "Low risk to the general population today and the need for long-term preparedness are not contradictory. CDC's latest assessment illustrates why preparedness must anticipate changes in infectious-disease transmission rather than react to them after they occur. We believe diversified vaccine supply and scalable MVA manufacturing capacity can become increasingly important as the epidemiology of mpox continues to evolve." A Changing Mpox Landscape The development is particularly noteworthy because the 2022 global mpox outbreak, including the large U.S. outbreak, was caused by Clade IIb. Clade I mpox has historically been associated with more severe disease and higher mortality than Clade II. However, disease severity varies by viral subclade, population and access to medical care. Recent Clade Ib cases identified in high-income countries have generally involved relatively mild illness, underscoring the importance of distinguishing the changing epidemiology of the virus from the immediate risk it poses to the general population. The significance of CDC's latest assessment therefore extends beyond disease severity alone. The emergence of likely sustained Clade Ib transmission represents an important change in the geographic footprint and transmission dynamics of mpox in the United States. The new CDC assessment also represents an evolution from earlier U.S. surveillance. As recently as August, CDC reported that sustained Clade Ib transmission had not been detected in the United States during 2024–2025. The September 25 assessment now indicates a likely transition toward sustained domestic transmission. Globally, Clade I outbreaks have continued in Central and Eastern Africa since late 2023, with subsequent geographic expansion beyond the region, including transmission in parts of Europe and introductions into the United States. The evolving epidemiology follows other recent public-health preparedness actions, including updated CDC vaccination recommendations for certain U.S. travelers at increased risk and international initiatives to strengthen access to mpox vaccines and outbreak-response capabilities. About GeoVax GeoVax Labs, Inc. is a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on the development of vaccines and immunotherapies addressing high-consequence infectious diseases and solid tumor cancers. GeoVax's priority program is GEO-MVA, a Modified Vaccinia Ankara (MVA)–based vaccine targeting mpox and smallpox. The program is advancing under an expedited regulatory pathway, with plans to initiate a pivotal Phase 3 clinical trial in the second half of 2026, to address critical global needs for expanded orthopoxvirus vaccine supply and biodefense preparedness. In oncology, GeoVax is developing Gedeptin(R), a gene-directed enzyme prodrug therapy (GDEPT) designed to enhance immune checkpoint inhibitor activity. Gedeptin has completed a multicenter Phase 1/2 clinical trial in advanced head and neck cancer and is being advanced into combination strategies, including planned neoadjuvant and first-line settings. GeoVax maintains a global intellectual property portfolio supporting its infectious disease and oncology programs and continues to evaluate strategic partnerships and funding opportunities aligned with its development priorities. For more information, visit www.geovax.com. Forward-Looking Statements This release contains forward-looking statements regarding GeoVax's business plans.
